complaints.title: Closure of the federal forum to persons of African descent

jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States

count.collective_note: Formally, every person of African descent then living in the United States, free or enslaved.

harmed.collective: Persons of African descent within the United States
harmed.interstitial: Every injury suffered by a person of African descent between 1857 and 1868 that went unheard because this holding closed the forum. Those injuries have no entries anywhere, and cannot be counted.

respondents.described: Chief Justice Roger B. Taney and the concurring majority, acting in judicial capacity

named.name: Roger B. Taney
named.role: Chief Justice of the United States; author of the opinion
named.note: Named as author of the holding. The conduct was lawful judicial action; no offence is charged in this entry.

process.forum: Supreme Court of the United States
process.narrative: No process was possible, because the holding was itself the act complained of. It is entered first in this book because it establishes the condition every earlier complaint was decided under and every later one had to overcome: not that the injury was excused, but that no forum would hear it.

escalation.note: Won at trial, reversed by the Missouri Supreme Court.

escalation.forum: U.S. Circuit Court, District of Missouri, 1854
Supreme Court of the United States, 1857
escalation.note: Held that he could not invoke the jurisdiction of any federal court. The ladder was climbed to the top rung and the top rung removed the ladder.

granted: Superseded by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments and the Civil Rights Act of 1866
remedy.outstanding: The decision was never overruled by the Court; it was displaced by constitutional amendment.

complaints.status_note: Citation: Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857).
complaints.offense_note: Not a violent act. The entry records a lawful judicial holding that operated as the precondition for the violence in every entry below. It is carried here because a log that recorded only the blows and not the rule that made them unanswerable would be incomplete.
complaints.conduct: The Court held that persons of African descent, whether enslaved or free, were not and could not become citizens within the meaning of Article III, and therefore could not invoke the jurisdiction of the federal courts; and further that Congress lacked power to prohibit slavery in the territories.

restoration.reached: No individual. The holding was displaced by constitutional amendment, which restored nothing to the Scotts.

concurrence.agree: The holding is the judicial record itself; there is no divergence as to what was decided.
concurrence.diverge: Sources diverge on Taney's motive and on whether the territorial holding was necessary to the judgment. The book does not resolve it.

complaints.title: The anti-literacy statutes: making the teaching of a child a crime

place.note: South Carolina from 1740, Georgia, North Carolina from 1830, Louisiana and Alabama from the 1830s, Virginia from 1831

complaints.conduct: Colonial and state legislatures made it a criminal offence to teach an enslaved person, and in several states any free Black person, to read or write. The statutes punished the teacher and, where the teacher was Black, the teacher's body: fines and imprisonment for white offenders, whipping for Black ones. Several were enacted directly after revolts - South Carolina's in 1740 after Stono, Virginia's in 1831 after Nat Turner - on the express reasoning that literacy made a person ungovernable.
complaints.offense_note: No offence is named. The conduct WAS the law: legislatures enacting statutes within their power. The entry records that the deprivation was deliberate, statutory, and aimed at children, and that no forum has ever been asked to answer for it.

count.note: Every enslaved child in the enacting states for the duration of the statutes, and free Black children in several of them. No figure is meaningful; the deprivation was universal within its jurisdictions.

harmed.collective: Enslaved and free Black children in the enacting states

children.carried_into_adulthood: A person kept from literacy as a child could not read a bill of sale, a labour contract, a ballot, or a summons as an adult. The statutes therefore reached forward into every later transaction that required reading, which is most of the ones this book records - including the sharecropping contracts of the Elaine entry and the mother's mark on the consent form in the sterilisation entry.

harmed.interstitial: The clandestine schools kept anyway - in kitchens, at night, in pits - and the risk borne by whoever taught. Frederick Douglass's account of Sophia Auld being ordered to stop, and of Hugh Auld's reasoning that literacy would forever unfit him to be a slave, is the clearest statement in the corpus of what the statutes were for.

transmitted.description: Emancipation found a population that had been kept from reading by law for a century and a half, and then held that population's literacy against it as a qualification for voting. Literacy tests in the disfranchising constitutions of the 1890s tested for a deficit the same legislatures had created.

respondents.described: Colonial assemblies and state legislatures; the courts that enforced the statutes and the officers who administered the whippings

process.narrative: No forum, then or since. The statutes were lawful exercises of legislative power and were displaced by emancipation rather than repudiated. No state that enacted one has treated it as a wrong requiring an answer, and no proceeding has ever been brought about them.

escalation.note: The legislature was the actor. There was no rung above it that would hear a complaint about its own statutes, and the people affected had no capacity to bring one.
The only proceedings that ever arose under these laws ran against the teachers and the learners.

restoration.reached: Nobody. The statutes lapsed with emancipation; nothing was restored and no state has acknowledged them as an injury.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

remedy.outstanding: Everything. The freedpeople's own response - the immediate, mass establishment of schools after 1865, often before anything else - is the measure of what had been withheld.

concurrence.agree: The statute books, the court records enforcing them, and the narratives agree completely. The legislatures wrote down what they were doing and why.
concurrence.diverge: They do not diverge on the fact. They diverge on the reason offered: the statutes cite public safety, the narratives describe the withholding of a capacity.

complaints.status_note: Entered to correct a gap this book reported on itself: educational harm appeared in two entries of twenty-two, which was a deficiency in the corpus rather than in the history. This is the foundational one, and it is aimed at children by design.

foreclosed_contribution.basis: Every enslaved child in the enacting states, for 125 years, kept from literacy by criminal statute — and free Black children in several of those states. The input destroyed is a whole population's access to written thought across five generations.
foreclosed_contribution.note: The book records the foreclosure and states its documentable magnitude. It does not record what would have been made. No entry here names a work, a discovery, an invention or an achievement that did not happen, and none ever will: a counterfactual asserted as evidence would be indistinguishable from the fabrications this book's entire evidentiary standard exists to exclude. What is recorded is the input that was destroyed, which is a fact. What it would have produced is unknowable, and the unknowability is itself the injury - it is not possible to say what was lost, and that is what makes the loss total rather than measurable.

complaints.title: Chattel enslavement in the United States and its colonial predecessors

place.note: The slaveholding colonies and states, and the domestic trade between them

count.note: Approximately 3.9 million persons were enslaved in the United States at the 1860 census. The number of persons enslaved across the full period is larger by an order that this book does not estimate.

harmed.collective: Enslaved persons in North America and their descendants
harmed.interstitial: Wealth transferred and still held. Names not preserved and now unrecoverable. Kinship lines severed by sale, which is why descendants of this entry frequently cannot document the ancestry that a claim would require of them.

transmitted.description: Kinship lines severed by sale, so descent cannot be documented by people from whom documentation is now demanded. Wealth transferred and compounding for a further eight generations. And the claim this book cannot itself establish: that trauma sustained across generations without opportunity to heal produces adaptive behaviours that outlive the conditions that required them - DeGruy's vacant esteem, ever-present anger, and racist socialisation. Her illustration is a mother who disparages her own child in front of a white observer, which reads as cruelty and originates as protection: under slavery and after it, a Black child who was visibly valued was a child in danger, so the parent learned to make the child appear worthless in order to keep them safe. DeGruy's point is that the behaviour survived the danger. The white parent in the same room is not performing that calculation and cannot see it being performed, which is why the two parents are described as raising children under conditions that look identical and are not.
transmitted.note: Standing is argued_in_literature, not documented. Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome is an influential and widely taught framework and is not a diagnostic category; parts of the transmission literature it draws on are actively contested. The book records the argument, names whose it is, and does not convert it into a finding. Note what is being recorded and what is not: that Black parents have described this protective calculation, and that DeGruy theorises its origin, are both matters of record. Whether the mechanism operates as she describes is her argument, and it is left as one.

children.carried_into_adulthood: A child sold from a parent lost the line of descent as well as the parent, and enters the record twice: once as property and once as an ancestor who cannot be traced. The condition was heritable through the mother by statute, so the injury began before birth.

respondents.described: Slaveholders; slave traders; sheriffs, patrols, and courts enforcing the slave codes; legislatures enacting them; insurers, banks, and shippers financing the trade

process.narrative: There was no forum. The conduct was lawful where it occurred and its victims lacked the legal capacity to complain of it. This entry exists because a log of unpunished crimes that omitted it on the ground that it was not then a crime would be reproducing the impediment rather than recording it.

escalation.forum: The holder, the overseer, the patrol
escalation.note: Discipline and killing were the holder's own prerogative. There was no rung above to appeal to, because the conduct was not an offence.
No legal capacity to complain, contract, or testify against a white person. The bar was the personhood rule, not a court's discretion.

sought: General Orders No. 15 (Special Field Orders No. 15), 1865, rescinded the same year
H.R. 40, introduced in every Congress since 1989, never enacted
granted: Abolition by the Thirteenth Amendment, which is not compensation
remedy.outstanding: No compensation was ever paid to any enslaved person by the United States. Compensation was paid to slaveholders in the District of Columbia under the Compensated Emancipation Act of 1862.

complaints.status_note: The register cannot be completed for this entry and never will be. Named individuals appear where a narrative, register, petition, or bill of sale preserved a name; the overwhelming majority did not. See PR-COLLECTIVE-ENSLAVED-US.
complaints.conduct: Holding of persons as property; compelled uncompensated labor; sale and separation of families; sexual violence without cognizable offense; killing and maiming under statutes that graded such acts as damage to property or excused them entirely; and denial of the legal capacity to testify, contract, marry, or sue.

restoration.reached: Nobody. No compensation was ever paid to any enslaved person by the United States; compensation was paid to slaveholders in the District of Columbia in 1862.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

concurrence.agree: Victim testimony, administrative record and the perpetrating institutions' own ledgers agree on the constituent conduct.
concurrence.diverge: The narrative corpus and the administrative corpus diverge systematically in what they record: the ledgers preserve numbers and prices, the narratives preserve names, kinship and violence. Neither is complete, and the ledger's completeness is a feature of who kept it.

foreclosed_contribution.basis: Approximately 3.9 million people at the 1860 census alone, whose working and creative lives were appropriated in their entirety. Whatever any of them would otherwise have made was foreclosed by the same act that appropriated the labour.
foreclosed_contribution.note: The book records the foreclosure and states its documentable magnitude. It does not record what would have been made. What is recorded is the input that was destroyed, which is a fact. complaints.title: The domestic slave trade: trafficking and forced displacement, 1808-1865

place.note: Upper South to Deep South: Virginia, Maryland and Kentucky to Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Texas, overland and by sea

complaints.conduct: Approximately one million people were bought in the Upper South and transported, in coffles overland and by ship along the coast, to be sold in the Deep South. Sales were transacted at arm's length between strangers, recorded in bills of sale, entered in county deed and probate books, insured, and pledged as collateral for loans. Families were separated as a routine incident of the business: spouses sold apart, children sold from parents.

count.note: Approximately one million people forcibly relocated over the period. Estimates of families broken vary; a commonly cited figure is that the trade destroyed something on the order of a third of enslaved marriages in the exporting states, and separated a comparable share of children from a parent. The book records the divergence rather than a single number.

harmed.collective: Enslaved people of the Upper South and the families left behind
harmed.interstitial: The letters written to find a sold spouse or child, and the advertisements placed in Black newspapers after emancipation by people searching for relatives sold decades earlier. Those advertisements are the trade's own casualty list, compiled by the victims, and they ran for forty years.

transmitted.description: Descent lines severed at the point of sale. A person sold from Maryland to Louisiana appears in two counties' records under two owners and often two names, so the genealogical thread breaks exactly where the trade cut it - which is why descendants today frequently cannot document the ancestry that a claim would require of them.

children.carried_into_adulthood: Children were a substantial share of those sold, and the post-emancipation advertisements placed by adults searching for parents and siblings sold decades earlier are the record of what that did to them across a lifetime.

respondents.described: Slave-trading firms, among them Franklin & Armfield of Alexandria, the largest in the trade; the sellers and buyers named in every bill of sale; the county clerks who recorded them; the banks that took enslaved people as collateral; the insurers who underwrote their lives; and the Customs Service, which required and retained a manifest for every person shipped coastwise.

named.name: Franklin & Armfield
named.role: Slave-trading firm, Alexandria, Virginia; the largest in the domestic trade
named.note: Named throughout its own surviving ledgers, correspondence and coastwise manifests. The firm was never charged with anything, because the business was lawful.

process.narrative: No forum, because the trade was lawful and its participants were engaged in commerce the law protected. The federal government did not prohibit it; it regulated it, requiring a manifest naming every person shipped coastwise and preserving those manifests in the customs records. That is the characteristic fact of this entry: the state's involvement was administrative rather than prosecutorial, and the paperwork it demanded is now the evidence.

escalation.note: The transaction was the conduct. There was no complaint to bring.
The county recorded the sale to make title good. It was the registrar of the conduct, not a forum for complaint about it.

escalation.forum: U.S. Customs Service, coastwise manifests required from 1808
escalation.note: Federal law required the manifest and the federal government kept it. The only rung of the ladder that touched this trade did so to document it.

restoration.reached: Nobody. No compensation was ever paid to any person trafficked in the domestic trade, and none has been sought in any forum that could grant it.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

remedy.outstanding: Everything. The proceeds of the trade capitalised banks, insurers, universities and estates whose successors exist; the manifests and deed books name both the people sold and the parties who profited.

concurrence.agree: The commercial record and the victim testimony agree completely on the conduct. Bills of sale, deed books, firm ledgers, coastwise manifests and insurance policies establish the transactions; the WPA narratives, the post-emancipation search advertisements, and narratives such as Northup's establish what the transactions did to the people inside them.
concurrence.diverge: They diverge on what the record is for. The commercial documents describe a lawful sale of property and are silent on everything the narratives are about. Neither is incomplete - each is a full account from its own vantage, and the distance between them is the finding.

complaints.status_note: Entered separately from chattel enslavement because the trade is a distinct course of conduct with a distinct and unusually complete documentary record. It is the entry in which the perpetrators' own instruments carry the proof: a bill of sale exists because title had to be provable, and it proves the transaction to us for the same reason it proved it to them.

foreclosed_contribution.basis: Approximately one million people relocated by force, and the households, apprenticeships and communities each removal dissolved.

complaints.title: The Clotilda: an Atlantic voyage that was a capital crime when it was made

place.note: Embarked from Ouidah, in present-day Benin

jurisdiction: United States District Court, Southern District of Alabama

complaints.conduct: Roughly 110 people were taken from Ouidah and carried to Mobile Bay in 1860, more than fifty years after the United States prohibited the international slave trade and forty years after Congress declared participation in it piracy punishable by death. The vessel was burned on arrival to destroy the evidence. The survivors were distributed among the financiers and, after emancipation, founded Africatown near Mobile.

count.note: Approximately 110 people; accounts differ by a few either way.

harmed.collective: The people carried on the Clotilda and the Africatown community they founded
harmed.interstitial: Survivors who had been taken as adults spent the rest of their lives among people who did not share their language, and several are recorded as wanting to return and never being able to afford passage.

children.carried_into_adulthood: Matilda McCrear was about two years old when she was carried to Alabama. She lived to 1940 and sought compensation in the 1930s; she was refused.

respondents.described: Timothy Meaher, who financed the voyage on a wager, and William Foster, who captained the vessel and burned it

named.name: Timothy Meaher
named.note: Federal proceedings were commenced and produced no conviction. The prosecution did not survive the onset of the Civil War, and the family remained prominent in Mobile.

named.name: William Foster
named.role: Captain of the Clotilda; burned the vessel to destroy the evidence
named.note: Left his own written account of the voyage.

process.forum: United States District Court, Southern District of Alabama
process.narrative: This is the entry in which the conduct was unambiguously a crime under United States law at the time it was committed - a capital one - and still produced no punishment. Federal proceedings were commenced and came to nothing; the outbreak of war ended them. The wreck was located and confirmed by the Alabama Historical Commission in 2019, and the descendants of the people carried on it and of the man who financed the voyage both still live in Mobile.

escalation.forum: United States District Court, Southern District of Alabama, 1860-1861
escalation.note: Commenced under statutes making the trade piracy. No conviction; the case did not survive the war.
Confirmed the identity of the wreck, 159 years after the voyage.

restoration.reached: No individual. The wreck was identified and Africatown has been recognised as a historic district; nothing was paid to the survivors, who lived into the 1930s, or to their descendants.

remedy.outstanding: Everything. Africatown today sits among heavy industry and has pressed for environmental and economic redress; the descendants of the people carried on the ship are identified and living.

concurrence.agree: The perpetrators' own accounts, the federal court papers, the survivors' testimony recorded by Zora Neale Hurston, and the physical wreck confirmed in 2019 all agree that the voyage happened and that it happened when it did.
concurrence.diverge: Accounts differ on the exact number carried and on why the prosecution failed. What does not differ is that the conduct was a capital offence under United States law and that nobody was punished for it.

complaints.status_note: Held against the rest of the corpus, this entry disposes of the objection that slavery's harms cannot be counted as crimes because they were lawful. Here the conduct was a capital crime when it was done, it was documented by its own perpetrators, and it was still unpunished.

foreclosed_contribution.basis: Roughly 110 people, taken as adults and children from a place with its own language, craft and learning, none of which survived the passage intact.

complaints.title: The 1838 Jesuit sale of 272 people to Louisiana

place.note: Sold from Jesuit plantations in Maryland to purchasers in Louisiana

complaints.conduct: The Maryland Province of the Society of Jesus sold 272 enslaved people from its plantations to purchasers in Louisiana. The sale was negotiated, papered, and executed by the institution; the proceeds relieved the debts of Georgetown College. Families were separated and the people sold were shipped south, in breach even of the conditions the order had set for itself about keeping families together and preserving religious practice.

count.note: 272 people named in the institution's own articles of agreement and associated records.

harmed.collective: The 272 and their descendants, who are identified and organised today

transmitted.description: Because the sellers recorded the names, the descent lines survive. Several thousand descendants have been identified and constitute an organised community - the inverse of the ordinary case in this book, where the absence of a name ends the line.

children.carried_into_adulthood: Families were separated in the execution of the sale notwithstanding the order's own stated conditions.

respondents.described: The Maryland Province of the Society of Jesus, which owned and sold the people; the purchasers Henry Johnson and Jesse Batey; and Georgetown College, whose finances the proceeds relieved

named.name: Maryland Province, Society of Jesus
named.note: Named in its own articles of agreement. The order acknowledged the sale in 2016 and apologised in 2017.

process.narrative: No proceeding, then or since. What distinguishes this entry is what the institution's own archive later made possible: because the sellers wrote down the names in order to convey title, descendants could be identified nearly two centuries later, and the identification is what forced the institutional response.

escalation.forum: The Society of Jesus and Georgetown College
escalation.note: Lawful sale; no complaint available to those sold.

escalation.forum: Georgetown University and the Society of Jesus, 2016-2021
escalation.note: Not adjudication. An institution acting on its own record after descendants used that record to identify themselves.

restoration.reached: Descendants, partially and by the institution's own choice rather than any order: a formal apology, renamed buildings, preferential admission consideration for descendants, and a foundation established with the Jesuits committing $100 million, funded over time. No court or legislature required any of it.

sought: Descendant organising and negotiation with Georgetown University and the Society of Jesus, 2015 onward
granted: Apology, 2017
Preferential admission consideration for descendants
Descendants Truth and Reconciliation Foundation, with a $100 million Jesuit commitment
remedy.outstanding: The commitment is being funded over time and descendants have publicly disputed its pace and terms. Nothing was compelled; a different institution facing the same record could have done nothing.

concurrence.agree: The institution's own articles of agreement, its correspondence, the ship manifests and the Louisiana records agree on the sale, the number, and the names.
concurrence.diverge: The order's internal correspondence records conditions it set for the sale - families kept together, religious practice preserved - which the execution did not honour. The gap between the institution's stated terms and its own records of what happened is documented in the same archive.

complaints.status_note: The clearest demonstration in the corpus of the point the domestic trade entry makes generally: the ledger kept to prove title is the evidence, and where the names survive, the claim survives with them. This is the only entry here in which a perpetrator institution's own record produced material restoration. Note on tagging: the proceeds financed a college, but that is the institution's gain rather than an educational injury to the people sold, so this entry does not carry the educational domain. Broadening it would have improved a coverage number the methodology says to fix by writing the missing entries instead.

complaints.title: Kidnapping of Solomon Northup and the failure of the prosecution

place.note: Kidnapped in Washington; held in Rapides and Avoyelles Parishes, Louisiana

harmed.collective: Free Black citizens of the northern states, of whom an unknown number were kidnapped and sold and never recovered
harmed.interstitial: Twelve years of a life. An unknown number of other free Black northerners kidnapped in the same trade who were never recovered and so left no narrative, no prosecution, and no entry.

respondents.described: James H. Birch, the trader who sold him in Washington; Alexander Merrill and Joseph Russell, charged in New York with the kidnapping

named.name: James H. Birch
named.note: Acquitted because Northup, the only witness, was barred by District law from testifying against him.

named.name: Alexander Merrill
named.note: Prosecuted in New York from 1854; the case ended without conviction after years of jurisdictional contest.

process.forum: Criminal court, District of Columbia (1853); Saratoga and Washington County courts, New York (1854-1857)
process.narrative: Birch was charged in Washington and acquitted. The reason is the whole of this entry: Northup, the only witness to his own kidnapping, was barred by District law from testifying against a white man. Birch was permitted to testify in his own defence. The subsequent New York prosecution of Merrill and Russell was obstructed for years by contests over jurisdiction between the two states and ended without a conviction.

escalation.note: Birch acquitted. Northup, the only witness, was barred by District law from testifying against him; Birch testified in his own defence.

escalation.forum: Saratoga and Washington County courts, New York, 1854-1857
escalation.note: Obstructed for years by contests over jurisdiction between two states, and abandoned.

sought: Criminal prosecution in the District of Columbia, 1853
granted: Recovery of his liberty, by executive action of the Governor of New York under an 1840 statute
remedy.outstanding: No conviction. No compensation for twelve years of uncompensated labour. Northup's own date and place of death are unknown.

complaints.status_note: Entered as the cleanest single illustration of the difference this book records. The crime was documented, the perpetrator was named, the forum was open, and the victim was silenced by a rule of evidence. Twelve Years a Slave (1853) is the complaint he filed instead, and it is the one that survived.
complaints.conduct: Solomon Northup, a free citizen of New York, was drugged, seized, held in a slave pen within sight of the Capitol, and sold south. He was held in slavery for twelve years until his identity was established and he was recovered by an agent of the Governor of New York.

restoration.reached: Solomon Northup alone, by executive action of the Governor of New York. No other kidnapped free northerner in the record was recovered.

concurrence.agree: Northup's narrative, the New York executive record and the District prosecution agree on the kidnapping and the twelve years.
concurrence.diverge: Birch's account, given in his own defence, contradicts Northup's throughout. It prevailed because Northup was barred from answering it, so the divergence was never tested on the evidence.

foreclosed_contribution.basis: Twelve years of one man's life, and the narrative he wrote afterwards is the only reason any of it is recoverable.

complaints.title: Colfax massacre and the reversal of the convictions

jurisdiction: United States (Circuit Court, District of Louisiana)

count.note: Counts vary by source. Most of the dead were killed after surrender.

harmed.collective: Black residents of Grant Parish
harmed.interstitial: The collapse of Reconstruction enforcement in Louisiana. Cruikshank's holding then travelled outward from these dead and disposed of prosecutions in states that had nothing to do with Grant Parish.

respondents.described: Members of the attacking force, including former Confederate soldiers and members of the White League

process.forum: United States Circuit Court, District of Louisiana; Supreme Court of the United States
process.narrative: Federal prosecutions under the Enforcement Act of 1870 produced three convictions. In United States v. Cruikshank, 92 U.S. 542 (1876), the Supreme Court set them aside, holding that the Fourteenth Amendment reached only state action and that the indictment failed to charge a federal offense. No one was ever punished for the killings.

escalation.note: No state prosecution was attempted.

escalation.forum: U.S. Circuit Court, District of Louisiana, 1874
escalation.note: Three convictions under the Enforcement Act of 1870.
Convictions set aside: the Fourteenth Amendment reached only state action, and the indictment charged no federal offence. The only convictions in the corpus were undone at the highest rung.

remedy.outstanding: None sought or obtained. A Louisiana state marker erected in 1950 described the event as a riot and was removed in 2021.

complaints.status_note: The controlling entry for the state action impediment: the case that created the doctrine is the case in which the only convictions were lost.
complaints.conduct: An armed white force attacked Black state militia and freedmen defending the Grant Parish courthouse following the disputed 1872 Louisiana election, and killed a large number of them, most after they had surrendered.

restoration.reached: Nobody. The 1950 state marker calling the killings a riot was removed in 2021, so even the symbolic record was withdrawn rather than corrected.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

concurrence.agree: Federal indictments, congressional inquiry and press across the political spectrum agree that a mass killing occurred and that most died after surrender.
concurrence.diverge: The count diverges from roughly 60 to 150. No source is independent of the fact that no official count was attempted.

complaints.title: Compulsory and coerced sterilisation of Black women and girls

place.note: Statutory eugenics programmes in some thirty states; documented concentrations in North Carolina, Virginia, Alabama and Mississippi

jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States

complaints.conduct: State eugenics boards and, later, federally funded family planning programmes sterilised women and girls without meaningful consent. Buck v. Bell (1927) upheld compulsory sterilisation and was never overruled. North Carolina's Eugenics Board operated from 1929 to 1974 and sterilised some 7,600 people, with Black women and girls sharply over-represented in its later decades. In Alabama in 1973 two Black girls aged fourteen and twelve were sterilised under a federally funded programme after their mother, who could not read, marked an X on a form she was given to understand authorised continued contraceptive injections.

count.note: 7,600 is the North Carolina programme alone. Estimates for all state eugenics programmes run to roughly 60,000-70,000 people nationally; the Relf litigation record indicated that federally funded programmes were sterilising on the order of 100,000-150,000 people a year, an unknown share of them coerced.

harmed.collective: Black women and girls sterilised under state eugenics programmes and federally funded family planning

children.carried_into_adulthood: A girl sterilised at twelve or fourteen carries the whole of the injury into an adulthood she did not consent to enter that way. The classification that selected many of them - feebleminded - was itself produced by the intelligence-testing apparatus applied to Black children in schools, so the school and the operating table were connected by a single pedagogy.

harmed.interstitial: The children not born, and the fact that the paperwork was in order in nearly every case. Consent was documented; it was the comprehension that was withheld.

transmitted.description: Lines of descent ended by operation. Unlike every other transmitted harm in this book, this one was designed to be transmitted by preventing transmission - the explicit object of a eugenics programme is that there be no next generation.

respondents.described: State eugenics boards; physicians and social workers who referred and performed; the federal agencies whose programmes funded the operations; and the Supreme Court, whose 1927 judgment authorised compulsory sterilisation and has never been overruled

process.forum: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia; state legislatures
process.narrative: No one was prosecuted anywhere. The Relf litigation in 1974 struck down the federal regulations and required genuine informed consent, which changed the practice going forward and returned nothing to the girls. North Carolina enacted a compensation programme in 2013 for surviving victims of its Eugenics Board - the only such programme of consequence - and by then most of those sterilised had died. Buck v. Bell stands.

escalation.note: Upheld compulsory sterilisation. Never overruled; the highest rung authorised the conduct rather than reviewing it.
The boards were lawfully constituted and acted within their statutes.

escalation.forum: Relf v. Weinberger, U.S. District Court, District of Columbia, 1974
escalation.note: Struck down the federal regulations and required informed consent. Prospective only; no damages, no penalty.
Payments to verified living victims of the state's Eugenics Board, thirty-nine years after it closed.

restoration.reached: Verified living victims of the North Carolina programme, under the 2013 statute - a small fraction of those sterilised, because the programme required survival to 2013 and proof. complaints.title: Prince Edward County closes every public school for five years

jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States

complaints.conduct: Rather than desegregate, the Prince Edward County Board of Supervisors refused to appropriate any money for public schools and closed the entire system for five years. White children continued their education at a private academy supported by tuition grants and tax credits. Black children in the county had no public schooling at all. Some were sent to relatives in other states, some were reached by improvised programmes, and many received no formal education for the whole period.

count.note: Roughly two thousand Black children of school age in the county over the five years. Precise figures vary with how partial schooling elsewhere is counted.

harmed.collective: The Black schoolchildren of Prince Edward County, known since as the Lost Generation

children.carried_into_adulthood: Children who lost five years of schooling did not get them back. Many never completed secondary education, and the county's Black adults carried measurably lower attainment and earnings for the rest of their working lives. This is the clearest single demonstration in the corpus of the point that the injury begins in childhood and is collected in adulthood.

harmed.interstitial: The children sent away to relatives in other states, who lost their families in order to keep their schooling, and those who stayed and lost the schooling instead. Neither loss appears in any tally.

respondents.described: The Prince Edward County Board of Supervisors, which refused the appropriation; the Commonwealth of Virginia, whose Massive Resistance programme and tuition-grant scheme financed the private alternative

process.forum: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Virginia; Supreme Court of the United States
process.narrative: The county's original school case was one of the five consolidated into Brown, and it began with a student strike led by a sixteen-year-old. After Brown the county closed the schools instead. In Griffin v. County School Board (1964) the Supreme Court held that the closure denied equal protection and ordered the schools reopened - nine years after Brown, and five years into the closure. No official was penalised. In 2004 Virginia created a scholarship programme for those denied schooling, and in 2008 the General Assembly expressed regret.

escalation.note: The board was the actor; it declined to appropriate and continued to decline.

escalation.forum: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Virginia
escalation.note: Litigation ran for years while the schools stayed shut.

escalation.note: Held the closure unconstitutional and ordered the schools reopened. A finding against the county - but no penalty on any official, and five years already gone.
Scholarship programme for those denied schooling; expression of regret. Forty years later, when most of the Lost Generation were past fifty.

restoration.reached: Some of the Lost Generation, through the Brown v. Board of Education Scholarship Program created in 2004 - tuition for adults returning to education, decades after the years that were taken. Nothing reached those who had died, and nothing compensated the lost earnings of a working life.

sought: Davis v. County School Board, consolidated into Brown
granted: Schools ordered reopened, 1964
Scholarship programme, 2004
Expression of regret, 2008
remedy.outstanding: The five years. Every measure granted was educational access offered to adults in place of the childhood schooling withheld.

complaints.title: Lynching of Michael Donald, and the destruction of the organisation that did it
complaints.conduct: Members of the United Klans of America, angered that a jury had failed to convict a Black defendant charged with killing a white police officer, went out to find and kill a Black man at random. They abducted Michael Donald, nineteen years old and walking home, beat him, cut his throat, and hanged his body from a tree on a residential street in Mobile.

harmed.collective: Black residents of Mobile, and every community the organisation operated in
harmed.interstitial: Mobile police initially pursued a theory that the killing was a drug dispute, which the family rejected and which delayed the investigation by months.

children.carried_into_adulthood: Michael Donald was nineteen, walking home.

respondents.described: James Knowles and Henry Hays, members of the United Klans of America, acting on the direction and in the culture of the organisation; Bennie Jack Hays, a UKA officer

claimed_sanction.asserted: The killing was carried out as a sentence. The organisation's members treated a jury's failure to convict as a wrong they were entitled to answer, and answered it by selecting a stranger and executing him.

named.name: Henry Francis Hays
named.note: Convicted of capital murder in Alabama in 1983 and executed in 1997.

named.name: James Knowles
named.note: Pleaded guilty to a federal civil rights violation, testified, and was sentenced to life.

process.forum: Mobile County; U.S. District Court, Southern District of Alabama; Alabama state courts
process.narrative: The only entry in this log in which perpetrators were convicted and the convictions stood. Knowles pleaded guilty federally and testified; Hays was convicted of capital murder and executed in 1997, the only white man executed in Alabama in the twentieth century for killing a Black person. Beulah Mae Donald then brought a civil action against the organisation itself, and in 1987 an all-white Mobile jury returned a verdict of $7 million against the United Klans of America, bankrupting it. Its headquarters was signed over to her.

escalation.note: An early theory that the killing was a drug dispute delayed the case; the family rejected it and pressed for federal involvement.

escalation.forum: FBI and U.S. Attorney, Southern District of Alabama
escalation.note: Knowles pleaded guilty to a federal civil rights violation and testified against Hays.
Hays convicted of capital murder; sentence carried out in 1997.

escalation.forum: Donald v. United Klans of America, U.S. District Court, 1987
escalation.note: A $7 million verdict against the organisation, which bankrupted it. A tort claim did what a century of criminal law had not.

restoration.reached: Beulah Mae Donald, who received the organisation's headquarters building and what its assets yielded. The sum was nominal against the verdict; what it purchased was the end of the organisation.

sought: Donald v. United Klans of America, civil action
granted: Two convictions, one execution
$7 million verdict; the United Klans of America dissolved
remedy.outstanding: The street where his body was hung was renamed for him in 2006. His mother died in 1988, the year after the verdict.

concurrence.agree: The trial records, the co-defendant's sworn testimony, the civil verdict and later scholarship agree in full on who did it and why.
concurrence.diverge: Accounts differ on how far up the organisation the direction ran, and on why the initial local investigation took the course it did.
